issues.issue: "the Business" is defined only as "jointly developing Spanish language and bilingual print and media business", a boundary-less description that must nevertheless carry the weight of the noncompetition covenant later in paragraph 2. Two sides could reasonably differ on whether a given media or advertising activity falls inside it.

LSB is made responsible for "managing the day-to-day operations", including hiring, yet the immediately following sentence of paragraph 1 requires that "all expenditures must be done with the concurrence of DMSA" and paragraph 4 bars any member from incurring costs except per the approved budget. The scope of her operational authority cannot be fixed without reconciling those provisions.

The capital obligation is measured only by "an amount that DMSA deems appropriate" and the parenthetical lets DMSA count its own travel, legal, accounting and internal "labor of management and staff" as contributed capital. Both the existence of any minimum obligation and what may be booked as capital (and later repaid ahead of members under paragraph 4) are open to competing readings.

Distribution is left to what "the board decides to distribute", which sits against the mandatory annual tax distribution in the next sentence and the mandatory waterfall in paragraph 4. Whether the board's discretion is unfettered or subject to those provisions is contestable.

This makes the annual tax distribution mandatory ("shall distribute each year at least enough cash"), but paragraph 4 places the identical tax distribution third in a waterfall, behind reimbursement of out-of-pocket costs and repayment of DMSA's initial capital. The two cannot both be applied when client receipts are exhausted at the earlier tiers.

The undertaking to "jointly pursue the Business" through the LLC is immediately undercut by the following sentences allowing DMSA and its principals to retain and originate media, advertising contracts and clients for their own benefit whether or not similar to the LLC's Business. Whether the joint-pursuit covenant retains any operative content is exactly the sort of whole-instrument tension a court must resolve.

The carve-out for interests "that are not and will not be part of the LLC's business, whether similar to the LLC's Business or not" cannot be squared with the preceding covenant that the parties "shall through the LLC jointly pursue the Business". Which sentence governs when DMSA takes a Spanish-language media opportunity is genuinely open.

The enumeration "business, advertising contracts, marketing contracts, or any other contracts" ends in an open catch-all whose reach against the listed specifics is uncertain (ejusdem generis). It is unclear whether "any other contracts" sweeps in every commercial opportunity or only contracts of the enumerated advertising/marketing kind.

The disclaimer of "any obligation" to originate business for the LLC stands against the next sentence, in which DMSA "does agree that it intends to use diligent efforts to direct appropriate business to the Company". Whether DMSA owes anything at all turns on reconciling the two.

The right to "retain existing and originate new media opportunities, advertising contracts and clients for its own benefit" is difficult to reconcile with the paragraph 2 covenant to jointly pursue the Business through the LLC and with the confidentiality of client lists in paragraph 5. A court would have to decide which prevails when the same client is pursued.

"does agree that it intends to use diligent efforts" is ambiguous between a binding promise and a mere statement of present intention, and "appropriate business" supplies no measurable benchmark. The opening qualifier "[w]ithout diminishing DMSA's rights under the foregoing language" deepens the doubt about whether anything is actually promised.

"diligent efforts" is undefined and the clause supplies no standard, quota or benchmark by which LSB's origination efforts could be measured. Its meaning is also coloured by the contrasting, weaker "intends to use diligent efforts" imposed on DMSA in the preceding sentence.

"such services" has no clear antecedent — it may mean only originating media and advertising contracts and clients, or all of LSB's publishing services — and "its principals" is meaningless applied to an individual. The restraint also has no time or geographic limit and turns on the elastic phrase "to the extent it relates to the Business".

The covenant bars LSB from any competing activity while the same paragraph expressly permits DMSA and its principals to retain and originate competing media and advertising business for their own benefit. The one-sided asymmetry invites construction against the drafter when the reach of the restraint is disputed.

"the staffs of DMSA and Dialogo" uses "Dialogo" as an entity distinct from DMSA, yet paragraph 1 gives "Dialogo" as the name of the LLC itself, so the sentence either refers circularly to the LLC's own staff or to LSB's pre-existing Dialogo publication. "[I]nitially" is also unbounded as to duration.

The reference to a separate "Dialogo" staff cannot be squared with paragraph 1, which names the new LLC "Dialogo" and says nothing about any pre-existing Dialogo business being contributed. Nothing else in the instrument identifies what that entity is or what its staff costs.

The waterfall directs that all client receipts be applied first to reimburse "any out of pocket costs" — without saying whose — and second to repay DMSA's initial capital, an amount DMSA alone "deems appropriate" under paragraph 1. Both tiers are open-ended in a way that could consume every dollar before the members are reached.

Placing the owners' tax distribution third, behind reimbursement of costs and repayment of DMSA's capital, conflicts with paragraph 1's unconditional command that the board "shall distribute each year at least enough cash" to cover the owners' tax liability. The two provisions cannot both be honoured in a year of thin receipts.

The prohibition turns entirely on "the approved budget", a term the Agreement never defines and for which it prescribes no preparation or approval mechanism. Whether any budget exists, and who approves it, is left wholly open.

The bar on incurring costs except per an approved budget must be reconciled with paragraph 1, which makes LSB responsible for day-to-day operations and hiring while requiring DMSA's concurrence in all expenditures. Which control mechanism governs a given expense is not resolved by the instrument.

The sentence is mechanically broken to the point of unintelligibility — it appears to say the LLC will not borrow but that borrowing may occur in future if approved by someone unnamed — so both the rule and the approving body are unascertainable. A court could only fix its meaning by construction.

The confidentiality undertaking is textually incomplete — it never identifies with any clarity what category of information "in connection with the Business" is to be kept confidential, and the sentence trails off. The scope of the obligation cannot be applied as written.

Nondisclosure is excused only with "the prior written consent of the LLC", but the LLC is not a party to this Agreement and no mechanism for giving that consent is provided; the clause also has no carve-out for publicly available information. Its practical operation is uncertain on its face.

The bar on using Proprietary Information — defined in the next sentence to include advertising and subscription client lists and prospects — sits awkwardly against paragraph 2, which lets DMSA and its principals retain and originate clients for their own benefit. Whether DMSA may exploit LLC client information for itself is left unresolved.

The definition is an unlimited enumeration ending in the sweeping residue "client provided information, documents and data", with no exclusion for information already public or independently known. The outer boundary of what counts as Proprietary Information is therefore contestable.

The parties merely agree to execute future articles of organization and an operating agreement "consistent with this Agreement" and containing unspecified "standard terms and conditions", leaving open whether essential terms remain to be agreed. Whether this is a binding contract or an agreement to agree turns on that language.

This contemplated further documentation — including the right-of-first-refusal agreement promised in paragraph 1 — leaves it uncertain whether the operative promises in paragraphs 1 through 5 bind before those documents are signed. The instrument as a whole gives no answer.
